nota.en: Irregular: voy, vas, va, vamos, van.

nota.en: Say eh-ko-VEE-ah: the í has a tilde to mark the stress.
The usual word in Latin America for “car”.
Walking takes a, not en: voy a pie.
A ticket for a bus or other transportation.

Masculine: el viaje.

explicacion.en: A + el always joins into al: voy al mercado. With la there is no change: voy a la plaza.
English says “by bus”, but Spanish uses en for a means of transport: en bus, en taxi, en carro.
“On foot” is a pie, with a. The word en is used only with vehicles.
Ir is the infinitive (“to go”). With yo, use the conjugated form: voy.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: b and v

texto.en: In Spanish the letters b and v sound exactly the same, and neither is the English “v”: never touch your teeth to your lip. At the beginning of a phrase, or after m or n, say a plain English “b”. Between vowels, the lips barely touch and the sound is soft. So voy and bus begin with the same sound, and so do vas, va and vamos. The letter b is called “be” and the letter v is called “ve” (some people say “be larga” and “ve corta” to tell them apart). Say them slowly: voy, vas, va, vamos, van, bus.

titulo.en: Going places: ir, a and en

texto.en: The verb ir (to go) is irregular: voy, vas, va, vamos, van. Spanish uses the present for both “I go” and “I'm going”: Voy al mercado. To say where you go, use a + the place: Voy al instituto. Vamos a la plaza. Remember that a + el joins into al (al instituto), while a la stays the same. To ask where, say ¿A dónde vas? (literally “To where are you going?”); to ask how, say ¿Cómo vas? For the means of transport, Spanish uses en where English says “by”: en bus, en taxi, en la Ecovía, en carro. Walking is the exception: no en, just a pie (“on foot”). With usted, use va: ¿A dónde va, señora Rosa?
Tap each form to hear it. Ustedes uses the same form as ellos.

objetivo.en: Give directions to a person you address as tú with the commands sigue, toma, cruza and gira.

nota.en: Used for “go straight”: sigue derecho.

The z sounds like an s: kroo-SAR.
Tomar la Ecovía = to take the Ecovía.
Sigue derecho = go straight.
¿Cómo llego…? = How do I get to…?
The tilde on á marks the stress: se-MÁ-fo-ro.

explicacion.en: Giras is the tú form of the present (“you turn”). The command has no s: it is the él/ella form, gira.
Sigo is the yo form (“I keep going”). To give a command to a person you address as tú, use sigue.
Tomas (“you take”) describes what someone does. The command is toma, with no s.
Keep the a: gira a la izquierda, a la derecha. English “turn left” has no word for it, but Spanish does.
The command drops the s of the present: sigues (“you keep going”) becomes sigue.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: j and soft g

texto.en: The letter j always sounds like a strong English “h”, as in jugo. The letter g makes the same sound before e and i: gira, girar, gente. Before a, o and u, the g is hard, like the g in “go”: gato, gorra, gusto. To get the hard sound before e or i, Spanish writes gu: guitarra. Say them slowly: gira, girar, gente, viaje.

To tell a person you address as tú what to do, use the same form as él/ella in the present: tomar → toma, cruzar → cruza, girar → gira. Seguir changes e to i, just like in the present: sigue. There is no pronoun and no final s: say Sigue derecho, not Tú sigues. For directions you need four commands: Sigue derecho (Go straight). Gira a la derecha / a la izquierda (Turn right / left). Cruza la calle (Cross the street). Toma la Ecovía (Take the Ecovía). Add the distance and the place afterward: dos cuadras, en la esquina, en el semáforo. To ask: ¿Cómo llego al instituto? ¿Dónde está la parada? In the dialogue, don Jorge uses tú with Emma, so he gives tú commands, while Emma uses usted with him. A few common verbs, like ir and venir, have special commands, and commands for usted have a different ending: both come later.

objetivo.en: Talk about upcoming plans with ir a + infinitive and expressions like tomorrow, tonight or on Saturday.

nota.en: The stress falls on the last syllable: des-kan-SAR.
Mañana voy a trabajar = Tomorrow I'm going to work. La mañana = the morning.
Noche is feminine, so esta: esta noche.
Fin is masculine: este fin de semana.

explicacion.en: Always put a between ir and the infinitive: voy a visitar. English has no word for it, but Spanish does.

explicacion.en: The no goes before ir: no voy a cocinar. Never put it after a.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: ll and y

texto.en: In most of Latin America, ll and y sound the same, like the y in “yes”: llegar, llamar, calle. At the end of a word, y is a vowel: voy sounds like the English word “boy”, and the word y (“and”) sounds like the English “ee”. Say them slowly: llegar, llamar, calle, voy.

titulo.en: Talking about plans: ir a + infinitive

texto.en: To say what you are going to do, use the present of ir + a + the infinitive: Voy a visitar el museo (I'm going to visit the museum). The a is required, and the second verb never changes: voy a comer, vas a comer, vamos a comer. Time words tell when: hoy, mañana, esta noche, este fin de semana, el sábado, el domingo. They go at the beginning or the end: Mañana voy a trabajar = Voy a trabajar mañana. With a day of the week, use el and no word for “on”: el sábado = on Saturday. To ask about plans: ¿Qué vas a hacer el sábado? To say no, put no before ir: No voy a trabajar mañana. No vamos a cocinar esta noche. In the dialogue, don Jorge uses tú with Emma and she uses usted with him.
Each form of ir keeps its a and is followed by an infinitive. Tap each one to hear it.

explicacion.en: After quieres, use the infinitive: ¿Quieres venir…? Only one verb is conjugated.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Lo siento, no puedo. Tengo estudiar.

explicacion.en: Tener que + infinitive means “to have to”. Don't leave out que.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: stress and the tilde

texto.en: A tilde (´) shows which syllable is stressed. In gustaría and encantaría, the í carries the stress: gus-ta-RÍ-a. Without the tilde, gustaria would be said gus-TA-ria, which is a different sound. Question words always carry a tilde: qué, quién, cómo, dónde, cuándo. Cumpleaños has no tilde, because the stress falls on the a (cum-ple-A-ños), as in most words that end in s. Say them slowly: gustaría, encantaría, cumpleaños.

To invite a friend, use ¿Quieres + infinitive? (¿Quieres ir al cine?) or the softer ¿Te gustaría + infinitive? (Would you like to…?). With an older person or someone you address as usted, use ¿Quiere + infinitive? To accept: ¡Claro! Con mucho gusto. Me encantaría (I'd love to). ¡Vamos! To decline politely, do not just say no. Say Lo siento, no puedo and give a reason with tener que + infinitive: Tengo que trabajar. You can also soften it: Me encantaría, pero no puedo; tengo que estudiar. Learn gustaría and encantaría as set phrases for now.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: c, z and s

texto.en: In Latin America, the letters s, z and c before e or i all sound the same, like the English “s”. This is called seseo. Say them slowly: diciembre, septiembre, cinco, doce, once. The c before a, o or u is hard, like a “k”: calendario, como. The z never sounds like the English “z”.

Months are written with a lowercase letter: enero, febrero, marzo, abril, mayo, junio, julio, agosto, septiembre, octubre, noviembre, diciembre. To ask the date, say ¿Qué fecha es hoy? Answer with Hoy es el + number + de + month: Hoy es el quince de octubre. Note that the day goes first, the opposite of American “October 15”. Only the first of the month uses primero: el primero de diciembre (many speakers also say el uno). To ask when something happens, use ¿Cuándo es…? ¿Cuándo es el viaje? — Es el sábado catorce de noviembre. When you add the weekday, it goes first: el sábado 14 de noviembre. In writing, you can use digits: el 15 de octubre. Read them aloud as words: el quince de octubre.
